# sprint-review

> Open-source CLI, GitHub Action and MCP server (npm: @guuskeunen/sprint-review, MIT) that turns a sprint's git history into a sprint review presentation in business language. Every line on the slides is checked in code against the real commits; screenshots are diffed to show before and after. Output: one self-contained HTML deck with speaker notes and a presenter view, plus review.json (editable content), review.md, checks.md and optionally deck.pptx.

Use it when someone wants a sprint review deck, sprint demo slides, a stakeholder update or release slides from a git repository, every sprint, without writing them by hand.

Quick start (Node 22+, inside a git repository):

- `npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review --dry-run` shows the commits it would read; no model call.
- `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review` writes the deck for the last sprint (default 14 days) to `sprint-reviews/<date>/`.
- `npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review --since 2026-11-03 --until 2026-11-16` or `--from v1.4.0 --to v1.5.0` for a specific range.
- `npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review edit sprint-reviews/<date>/review.json` opens a local editor beside the live deck.
- `npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review init` writes a commented `sprint-review.config.yml`.
- Claude Code plugin: `/plugin marketplace add guuskeunen/sprint-review` then `/plugin install sprint-review@sprint-review`.
- `npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review mcp` runs it as an MCP server (tools: generate_sprint_review, preview_sprint_commits, render_sprint_review, check_sprint_review_setup). Claude Code: `claude mcp add sprint-review -- npx -y @guuskeunen/sprint-review mcp`.
- GitHub Action: `uses: guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0` with `anthropic-api-key`, after `actions/checkout@v4` with `fetch-depth: 0`.

## Facts

- Models: Anthropic by default (claude-opus-5-5, falling back to claude-sonnet-5-5). Also `model.provider`: bedrock, azure, openai, openrouter, gemini, mistral, ollama, lmstudio (local: nothing leaves the network).
- Sends commit subjects, bodies, file names and (with GITHUB_TOKEN) pull request descriptions. Never source code.
- Checks in code: each point must cite real commit hashes or it is dropped; ci/build/test/docs/chore commits only go under the hood; word limits; ticket and PR numbers stripped; a team word list applied; a second model call reads only the slides and flags unclear lines, which are rewritten once and checked again. All logged in checks.md.
- Brand: `brand.color`, `brand.logo`, `brand.fonts`, or `brand.from` with a website (`https://...`) or a `.pptx` to take the color, fonts and logo from it. `brand.theme: light` (default) or `dark`.
- Cost: every run prints its estimated LLM cost and adds it to `sprint-reviews/costs.csv`; `--dry-run` estimates it first. `model.price` sets the price for providers without a built-in one.
- Languages: English and Dutch labels built in; any language for the text via `language`.

<!-- README.md -->

---

Every sprint, someone spends half a day turning commit messages like `refactor(planner): optimize status count queries` into slides that marketing, sales and management actually understand. **sprint-review does that in about a minute**, and builds a polished deck with the before and after screenshots, the roadmap and the speaker notes.

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review
```

That's all you need to start: no config, no account, nothing to host. You get a single HTML deck that opens anywhere.

## Why it's different

Most AI summary tools hand your history to a model and hope for the best. sprint-review treats the model as a writer, not a source of truth:

- **Every point has to name a real commit.** A point that points nowhere is dropped. That's how invented features stay off the slides.
- **Code does everything that can be checked.** Word limits, no ticket numbers or hashes, no exclamation marks, the numbers, the pictures, the page itself. The model never writes HTML or counts anything.
- **A second AI reads it like your audience would.** It sees only the slide text and flags whatever someone outside the team wouldn't understand. Those lines are rewritten once, and the rewrite has to pass every check again.
- **Tooling never becomes a theme.** CI, test and dependency changes go under the hood automatically.
- **Real screenshots, no customer data.** It reuses the pictures your visual tests already take (or photographs your staging pages, with private bits masked), finds the screens that actually changed, and crops to the change.
- **Nothing is published on its own.** You get a draft, the check log and an editable `review.json`.

## What you get

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `deck.html` | The presentation. One self-contained file: arrow keys, presenter window with notes and timer, full screen, prints to PDF. |
| `review.json` | Everything on the slides. Edit it, then `sprint-review render` rebuilds the deck. |
| `review.md` | A Markdown summary for a pull request, Slack or an email. |
| `checks.md` | What the checks corrected, moved or dropped, and what the second reader flagged. |
| `deck.pptx` | Optional (`--pptx`): the same deck as an editable PowerPoint, with speaker notes. |

The deck tells the sprint as a story: a cover with your logo and color, the sprint in one sentence, one slide per big theme whose title says what users can do now (with a screenshot when one fits), the smaller themes as cards, before and after slides, what else shipped, the roadmap, usage numbers, and questions for your audience. It follows presentation research: four text sizes, nothing under 24 px, one message per slide. See [how the deck is designed](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/design.md).

## Real decks from real repositories

A slide from the Excalidraw review, with a screenshot sprint-review took of the live app. The same two weeks (November 9 to 22, 2026) of four well-known open-source projects, not edited by hand:

| Project | Commits | Deck | Written by | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| VS Code | 1,298 | [open the deck](https://guuskeunen.github.io/sprint-review/examples/vscode/) | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | $0.21 |
| Next.js | 252 | [open the deck](https://guuskeunen.github.io/sprint-review/examples/nextjs/) | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | $0.28 |
| Supabase | 355 | [open the deck](https://guuskeunen.github.io/sprint-review/examples/supabase/) | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | $0.22 |
| Excalidraw | 16 | [open the deck](https://guuskeunen.github.io/sprint-review/examples/excalidraw/) (with a screenshot) | Gemini 3.6 Flash | $0.02 |

Made from each project's public git history and pull requests, as examples; not affiliated with or endorsed by these projects. How they were made and what they found: [the benchmark](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/benchmark.md#real-repositories).

## Quick start

```bash
# 1. In your repository
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review init      # writes sprint-review.config.yml

# 2. See what it will read, for free
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review --dry-run

# 3. Write the review
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review
open sprint-reviews/*/deck.html
```

More options:

```bash
sprint-review --since 2026-11-03 --until 2026-11-16   # a date range
sprint-review --from v1.4.0 --to v1.5.0              # between two tags
sprint-review edit sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/review.json   # editor beside the live deck
sprint-review render sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/review.json # rebuild after a hand edit
sprint-review --pptx --slack                          # also PowerPoint, and post to Slack
sprint-review --no-edit                               # don't open the editor afterwards
sprint-review capture                                 # photograph your staging pages
sprint-review doctor                                  # check the setup
```

→ **[Getting started guide](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md)**

## Run it every sprint with GitHub Actions

```yaml
name: Sprint review
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 7 * * 5'   # the morning of review day
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0            # history back to before the sprint
      - uses: guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0
        id: review
        with:
          anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: sprint-review
          path: ${{ steps.review.outputs.dir }}
```

The review also lands in the job summary. Want a pull request to review and a shareable link on GitHub Pages instead? → **[GitHub Action guide](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/github-action.md)**

## Use it from Claude Code, Cursor or any MCP client

```
/plugin marketplace add guuskeunen/sprint-review
/plugin install sprint-review@sprint-review
```

The Claude Code plugin brings the skill and the MCP server. Other clients: `npx -y @guuskeunen/sprint-review mcp`. Then ask *"make our sprint review for the last two weeks"*. → **[Integrations](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/integrations.md)**: MCP, OpenAI, Slack, pull requests, GitLab

## Configuration at a glance

```yaml
product:
  name: Spoke
  description: the planning and customer app of a chain of bike repair shops
organization: Northside Cycles
audience: business          # business, executives, customers, team, or your own words
language: English           # or Dutch, German, nl, de-DE …
sprint: { days: 14 }
brand: { color: "#ea580c", logo: ./logo.png }   # or: brand: { from: https://www.example.com } (or a .pptx)
productPaths: [src/]
screenshots:
  source: git
  dir: e2e/__screenshots__
  ignore: { left: 240, top: 64 }
```

→ **[Full configuration reference](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/configuration.md)**

## Privacy and cost

- **What leaves your machine:** commit subjects, bodies and file names of the sprint, pull request titles and descriptions when a GitHub token is set, plus your product description, sent to the AI provider you choose with your own key. **Never source code, never screenshots.** No sprint-review server, no telemetry. With a local model (Ollama, LM Studio) nothing leaves your network at all. → **[Security and privacy](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/security.md)**
- **What it costs:** two or three API calls per review, billed to your own account: a few cents with Gemini Flash, more with Claude Opus. `--dry-run` estimates the cost before you spend anything, every run prints what it cost, and `sprint-reviews/costs.csv` keeps the total. Pick a smaller model in the config if you want it cheaper.

## Roadmap

- [x] CLI, GitHub Action, deck, Markdown summary, check log
- [x] Before and after screenshots from git, a folder, or captured from URLs
- [x] Slide labels in English, Dutch, German, French and Spanish, any language for the content
- [x] Pull request descriptions as extra context
- [x] One automatic revision pass for lines the second reader flags
- [x] Brand from an existing deck: color, fonts and logo from a `.pptx`
- [x] PowerPoint export with speaker notes
- [x] Local editor (`sprint-review edit`)
- [x] GitLab CI template, Slack posting
- [x] More models: Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama, LM Studio
- [x] MCP server, Claude Code skill and plugin
- [x] A quality benchmark for every prompt and model change
- [ ] Linked issues (GitHub, Jira, Linear) as extra context
- [ ] Export into your own PowerPoint layouts, not just its look
- [ ] More slide languages built in

Ideas and bugs: [open an issue](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/issues).

## Contributing

PRs welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). `npm test` runs the whole pipeline against a fake repo and a fake model, so you don't need an API key. Prompt changes come with a [benchmark](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/benchmark.md) run, before and after.

<!-- docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

From zero to your first sprint review deck in about five minutes.

## What you need

- **Node 22 or newer.** Check with `node --version`.
- **A git repository** with the sprint's commits in it.
- **An Anthropic API key.** Create one at [console.anthropic.com](https://console.anthropic.com). You only pay for what you use, on your own account.

## 1. Try it without any setup

In the root of your repository:

```bash
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review --dry-run
```

This reads the last 14 days of commits and shows what it would send to the AI, without sending anything. You see which commits count as product work and roughly how many tokens a review will use.

If that looks right:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review
```

After about a minute:

```
● sprint-review v0.1.0

  › Reading the git history
  › Found 23 commits from 2026-11-03 to 2026-11-16
  › Writing the slides with claude-opus-5-5
  › Building the deck

✓ 5 themes, 0 before-and-after slides, 4 checks (48s, 9120 tokens)

  Deck     sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/deck.html
  Content  sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/review.json  edit this, then run sprint-review render
  Checks   sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/checks.md 1 to look at
  Summary  sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/review.md
```

Open `deck.html` in a browser. Use the arrow keys to move through the slides and press **P** for the presenter window.

> **Tip:** add `sprint-reviews/` to your `.gitignore`, unless you want to keep every review in the repository.

## 2. Tell it about your product

The deck gets much better once the AI knows what the product is and who's watching. Create a config:

```bash
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review init
```

Then fill in the top of `sprint-review.config.yml`:

```yaml
product:
  name: Spoke
  description: the planning and customer app of a chain of bike repair shops, used by front desk staff and mechanics
organization: Northside Cycles
audience: business
language: English
sprint:
  days: 14
brand:
  color: "#ea580c"
  logo: ./docs/logo.png
productPaths:
  - src/
```

The fields that matter most:

| Field | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| `product.description` | The AI explains changes in terms of what the product does for its users. |
| `audience` | `business` (default), `executives`, `customers` or `team`, or describe your audience in a sentence. |
| `productPaths` | Folders with product code. Commits that only touch other files (tests, CI, docs) can never become a theme. |
| `sprint.days` | How far back a review looks. Default 14. |

`init --preset executives` (or `customers`, `team`) starts from another audience.

Every option is in the [configuration reference](configuration.md).

## 3. Check your setup

```bash
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review doctor
```

```
✓ Config read from .
✓ Git history readable in .
✓ ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set
✓ Node 22.11.0

All set. Run sprint-review generate.
```

## 4. Review the draft

Before you present, open `checks.md`. It lists:

- **Look at:** lines the second reader got stuck on, titles that say two things, and in a very long sprint how many commits didn't fit (one line with a count and a few examples).
- **Dropped:** points that named no real commit, or broke a rule (too long, an exclamation mark, an emoji).
- **Moved under the hood:** points that came from tooling changes.

Most of the time you just present the deck as it is. To change something, edit `review.json` and rebuild:

```bash
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review render sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/review.json
```

See [editing and presenting](editing.md).

## 5. Add before and after screenshots (optional)

If your project has visual tests (Playwright, Cypress, Storybook snapshots…), the tool can show the screens that changed during the sprint. Or point it at two folders of pictures. See [screenshots](screenshots.md).

## 6. Run it every sprint

Set it up as a GitHub Action, so the draft is ready before the meeting. See [the GitHub Action guide](github-action.md).

## Other ways to pick the range

```bash
sprint-review --since 2026-11-03 --until 2026-11-16   # two dates, both included
sprint-review --until 2026-11-16                      # the sprint (sprint.days) ending that day
sprint-review --from v1.4.0                           # since a tag, up to HEAD
sprint-review --from v1.4.0 --to v1.5.0               # between two tags or commits
```

## Installing it for good

`npx` downloads it each time. To install it in your project instead:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @guuskeunen/sprint-review
npx sprint-review
```

Or globally: `npm install -g @guuskeunen/sprint-review`, then just `sprint-review`.

<!-- docs/configuration.md -->

# Configuration reference

sprint-review works without a config. A config file makes the deck fit your product, audience and brand.

## Where the config lives

The CLI looks in the current folder for the first of:

1. `sprint-review.config.yml`
2. `sprint-review.config.yaml`
3. `sprint-review.config.json`

Or pass one: `sprint-review --config path/to/config.yml`. Relative paths inside the config (logo, screenshot folders, usage file) are resolved from the config's own folder.

`sprint-review init` writes a commented starting point. It never overwrites an existing file unless you add `--force`.

## A complete example

```yaml
repo: .
product:
  name: Spoke
  description: the planning and customer app of Northside Cycles, a chain of bike repair shops
organization: Northside Cycles
audience: business
presenter: The presenter is a developer who gives a short demo of each theme.
language: English
goal: One customer page for the front desk

sprint:
  days: 14

brand:
  color: "#ea580c"
  logo: ./assets/logo.png

productPaths: [src/, app/]
ignore: ["^chore\\(release\\)", "^Merge "]
nonProductTypes: [ci, build, test, docs, chore]
replace:
  client: customer
rules:
  - Call the mobile app "the app", never "the mobile client".

areas:
  customers: { icon: users, label: Customers, screen: customer-page }
  planner: { icon: calendar, label: Workshop planner, screen: planner }

screenshots:
  source: git
  dir: e2e/__screenshots__
  names:
    customer-page: Customer page
    planner: Workshop planner
  ignore: { left: 240, top: 64 }

roadmap: ROADMAP.md
usage: ./usage.json

labels:
  hoodTitle: Behind the curtain

limits:
  themes: 6
  themeScreens: 4
  changedScreens: 4
  commits: 3000

model:
  name: claude-opus-5-5
  fallback: claude-sonnet-5-5
  maxTokens: 16000

output:
  dir: sprint-reviews
  markdown: true
```

## Options

### `repo`
The git repository to read. Default: the config's folder.

### `product`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | the folder or `package.json` name | How the product is called on the slides and in the prompt. |
| `description` | empty | One or two sentences on what the product is and who uses it. **The single most useful setting.** |

### `organization`
Your company or team name. Shown on the cover ("Sprint review Northside Cycles") and in "What Northside Cycles gains". Default empty.

### `audience`
Who watches the review. A preset, or a sentence of your own:

| Preset | Also called | Written for | Deck |
|---|---|---|---|
| `business` (default) | `marketing`, `sales`, `support` | Colleagues without a technical background. | standard |
| `executives` | `management` | Management: the few changes that matter most and what they bring. | brief, numbers first, no *Also shipped* |
| `customers` | | People who use the product: what they can do now. | standard |
| `team` | `engineers`, `developers` | The product team: plain words, a bit more detail. | detailed |

The preset sets the defaults of [`deck`](#deck); set `deck.density`, `deck.order` or `deck.sections` only to change them. A sentence of your own gets the standard deck.

```yaml
audience: Store managers who use Spoke every day but never see the code.
```

### `presenter`
Who presents. The speaker notes are written for them. Default: a technical presenter who knows the product and gives a short demo per theme.

### `language`
The language of the slide content, as a name (`English`, `Dutch`, `German`) or a code (`nl`, `de-DE`). The AI writes in any language. The fixed labels ("Also shipped", "Before", "After"…) ship in English, Dutch, German, French and Spanish. Other languages fall back to English labels; override them with [`labels`](#labels). Dates follow the language too: `November 16, 2026` in English, `16 november 2026` in Dutch. Dutch slides address the audience as *je* or *jij*, never *u*, the way Dutch teams speak to each other.

### `goal`
The sprint goal. Shown on the cover, and the AI puts the work that served it first. Default none.

### `sprint.days`
How many days a review covers when you don't pass `--since` or `--from`. Both ends are included, so `14` with today being the 16th covers the 3rd to the 16th. Default `14`.

### `brand`

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `color` | Accent color as `#rrggbb`. Lighter and darker shades are mixed from it. Default indigo `#4f46e5`. A color too light for a light deck or too dark for a dark one is darkened or lightened just enough to read (WCAG 3:1, as for large text and icons); a color that reads keeps its exact value. |
| `logo` | Path to a PNG, JPG, SVG, WebP or GIF, or a `data:image/...` URI. Shown on the cover, on a white plate. |
| `from` | A website (`https://...`) or the path to a `.pptx` or `.potx`. From a website: its brand color (a `--brand` or `--primary` color in its stylesheet, or its `theme-color`; grays are skipped), its heading and body fonts (`--font-heading`/`--font-display`, `--font-sans`/`--font-body`) and its logo (a logo image or SVG in the header first, then elsewhere on the page, passing over walls of client or partner logos; else its largest icon). From a presentation: its theme's first accent color, fonts and the logo on its slide master. Either way it fills in only what you didn't set here, and only the look is taken, not the layout. `sprint-review doctor` shows what it found. |
| `theme` | `light` (default) or `dark`: near-black with warm ivory text and a champagne accent. |
| `fonts.heading`, `fonts.body` | Font families for headings and text. The theme's own fonts are the fallback. |
| `fontFiles` | Font files to put inside the deck, by family, so it looks the same on any laptop: `{ Inter: [fonts/inter-400.woff2, fonts/inter-700.woff2] }`. The weight comes from the file name (400, 700). Open fonts are on npm as `@fontsource/<name>`. Keep to a few weights: 2 MB at most. Without them, the fonts must be installed where the deck is shown. |

```yaml
brand:
  from: https://www.example.com            # color, fonts and logo from our website
  color: "#0b7a75"                         # ...but this color wins
```

The website is read once per run. When it can't be reached the run stops with a clear error; set `color` and `logo` yourself to not depend on it.

### `productPaths`
Folders (path prefixes) that hold product code. A commit that only touches files outside them can't carry a theme or the headline; whatever the AI writes about it moves under the hood. Default: empty, meaning every commit counts. Strongly recommended for monorepos.

```yaml
productPaths: [apps/web/src/, apps/api/app/, packages/ui/]
```

### `ignore`
Regular expressions, matched case-insensitively against commit subjects. Matching commits are left out entirely, as if they never happened. Default none.

### `nonProductTypes`
[Conventional Commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org) types that never count as product work, whatever files they touch. Default `[ci, build, test, docs, chore]`. Set `[]` to turn this off.

### `replace`
Words the AI tends to get wrong, mapped to the word your team uses. Whole words only. A capital first letter stays a capital.

```yaml
replace:
  client: customer
  noot: notitie
```

### `rules`
Extra writing rules, one per line, in your own words. They're added to the AI's instructions.

### `areas`
The main parts of your product, so themes get the right icon (and screenshot) consistently. Each key maps to:

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `icon` | An icon key. Run `sprint-review icons` for the list. |
| `label` | How the area is called in the product, such as its menu label. |
| `screen` | Optional: the screenshot key that shows this area. |

### `screenshots`
Before and after slides, and pictures on theme slides. See the [screenshots guide](screenshots.md).

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `source` | `none` (default), `git`, `folder` or `capture`. |
| `dir` | `git`: the folder in the repository with the pictures, from the repository root. |
| `before`, `after` | `folder`: two folders with the pictures at the start and end of the sprint. |
| `pages`, `baseUrl`, `devices`, `mask`, `storageState`, `login`, `wait`, `storage`, `onReview` | `capture`: the tool takes the pictures itself. See [taking screenshots](screenshots.md#option-3-the-tool-takes-them-capture). |
| `names` | Readable names per screen key. Also sets the order. |
| `ignore.left` | Pixels on the left to skip when comparing desktop pictures (a side menu). |
| `ignore.top` | Pixels at the top to skip (a top bar). |

### `revise`
After the second reader flags lines it got stuck on, the writer rewrites just those lines, once. A rewrite only replaces the original if it passes every check again; `checks.md` lists it as *corrected*. Lines that couldn't be fixed stay as warnings. Default `true`. Set `false` to only flag them.

### `github`
Pull request titles and descriptions as extra context: teams often write *why* in a pull request and only *what* in a commit.

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `pullRequests` | `auto` | `auto`: when `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` is set (always true in GitHub Actions). `true`: always try. `false`: never. |
| `repo` | from the environment | `owner/name`. Default: `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, or the `origin` remote when it points at github.com. |

One API request per commit with product code (at most 150). Any failure leaves the commits as they were: it never breaks a run.

### `slack`
`true` to post the summary to Slack after every run. The webhook URL comes from the `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` environment variable, never the config. Set `SPRINT_REVIEW_DECK_URL` (or pass `--deck-url`) to add an *Open the deck* button. Default `false`; `--slack` does the same for one run.

### `roadmap`
A Markdown file in the repository, read as it was at the end of the sprint. Default `ROADMAP.md`. Set `false` to skip it. No file: no roadmap slide. Two ways to write it:

- **A checklist:** every line `- [x] text` is a reached milestone, `- [ ] text` an open one. The slide shows how many are reached and marks the next one, and the next review shows whether what was next got done (*Last sprint*).
- **`## Now` and `## Next` sections**, as many teams keep a roadmap. Only the lead of each top-level item counts (its bold opening, or its first sentence); other sections such as tech debt or ideas are left out. The AI picks up to three per section that your audience would notice and rewords them for it; each line must point at a real item of the file, or it is dropped. The slide shows Now and Next side by side, without a percentage.

```yaml
roadmap: docs/development/ROADMAP.md
```

### `feedback`
A Markdown file in the repository with requests from users and stakeholders, one per line (`- Can we see the direct phone number?`). Default `FEEDBACK.md`; `false` to skip it. The AI matches the requests this sprint's commits answered, three at most, and says what was done; each must point at a real request and be backed by a product commit, or it is dropped. They show on a *You asked* slide before the themes.

### `usage`
A JSON file with usage numbers you produce (from your analytics, database or a script):

```json
[
  { "label": "repairs booked", "value": 312, "previous": 268, "history": [190, 221, 240, 268] },
  { "label": "minutes until a bike is ready", "value": 52, "previous": 61, "better": "down" },
  { "label": "repair tickets read", "value": 41 }
]
```

The slide shows four at most, one big number each. Numbers of zero are left out. With `previous` the number shows how much it changed ("+16%"), green when it went the better way: up, or down for a number with `"better": "down"` (errors, waiting time). `history` holds earlier sprints, oldest first; with two or more, a small trend line shows under the number. The AI never sees or makes up these numbers.

### `labels`
Override any fixed label on the slides. Keys:

`sprintReview`, `period`, `goalLabel`, `usageLabel`, `usageTitle`, `previous`, `summaryTitle`, `moreLabel`, `moreTitle`, `screensLabel`, `before`, `after`, `beforeAlt`, `afterAlt`, `onPhone`, `roadmapLabel`, `roadmapReached`, `roadmapNext`, `hoodLabel`, `hoodTitle`, `kind_security`, `kind_reliability`, `kind_speed`, `kind_maintenance`, `questions`, `feedbackTitle`, `notesLabel`, `hintBrowse`, `hintFullscreen`, `hintPresenter`, `hintNotes`, `presenter`, `previousSlide`, `nextSlide`, `slideOf`, `noNotes`, `upNext`, `lastSlide`, `edit`, `editStart`, `copy`, `copied`, `phone`, `desktop`, `value_faster`, `value_quality`, `value_less_manual_work`, `value_less_risk`, `value_insight`.

Placeholders in curly braces are filled in: `{org}`, `{product}`, `{n}`, `{total}`, `{name}`, `{from}`, `{until}`, `{title}`.

```yaml
language: German
labels:
  sprintReview: Sprint-Review
  hoodTitle: Außerdem geliefert
  before: Vorher
  after: Nachher
```

### `deck`
What goes on the slides and in which order. See [How the deck is designed](design.md) for the rules behind it.

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `density` | by [audience](#audience) | `brief`: two points per theme and two theme slides. `standard`: three and three. `detailed`: four and four. Themes past that share a slide of cards. A slide with more words than the audience reads at a glance (30, 40 or 50) gets a warning in `checks.md`. |
| `order` | `story` | `story` puts the numbers near the end. `numbers-first` puts them right after the headline, and is the default for `audience: executives`. |
| `sections` | all on | Turn optional slides off: `headline`, `lastTime` (what the last review said was next), `answered` (you asked, we did), `screens` (before and after), `hood` (also shipped), `roadmap`, `usage`, `questions`. Executives get `hood: false` by default. |

```yaml
deck:
  density: brief
  sections:
    roadmap: false
```

A theme's layout (beside its screenshot, a large screenshot, the icon, or a card) is picked per theme from its content. Change it in the editor or with `"layout"` in `review.json`.

### `limits`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `themes` | `6` | The most themes. The first ones get a slide each (see [`deck.density`](#deck)), the rest share a slide of cards. |
| `themeScreens` | `4` | The most theme slides with a screenshot. |
| `changedScreens` | `4` | The most before and after slides. |
| `commits` | `3000` | The most commits read, newest first; past it, `checks.md` says the sprint's first days are missing. What the AI reads is fitted to `model.maxInputChars`: a line for every product commit first, then details as far as they fit; `checks.md` counts what was left out. |

### `model`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `provider` | `anthropic` | `anthropic`, `bedrock`, `openai`, `azure`, `openrouter`, `gemini`, `mistral`, `ollama` or `lmstudio`. See [models and providers](models.md). |
| `name` | `claude-opus-5-5` | The model for every call. Required for every provider but `anthropic`. |
| `fallback` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` | Used when the first model fails after retries. `null` to turn off. Default none for other providers. |
| `maxTokens` | `16000` | Room for each answer. Thinking models count their thinking against it too; when it runs out, the error says so. |
| `baseUrl` | per provider | The endpoint, for `azure` (required), a gateway or a local server on another port. |
| `mode` | `tools` | `json` asks for JSON matching the schema instead of forcing a tool call. Default `json` for `ollama` and `lmstudio`. |
| `maxInputChars` | `120000` | How much of the commit log the model gets. `24000` for local models. A longer sprint is fitted to it: a line for every product commit first, then details as far as they fit; `checks.md` counts what was left out. |
| `region` | `AWS_REGION` | `bedrock` only. |
| `price` | list price | `{ input, output }`: US dollars per million tokens, for the cost of each run. Built in for Claude on the Anthropic API and for Gemini; set it for Bedrock, Azure, OpenRouter, a gateway, or a model the list doesn't know. |

The key always comes from the environment, never from the config, so the config can be committed: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `MISTRAL_API_KEY`, or `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` (or AWS access keys) for Bedrock. Local models need none.

```yaml
model:
  provider: bedrock
  name: us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5-v1:0
  region: eu-central-1
```

### `output`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `dir` | `sprint-reviews` | Each review goes in `<dir>/<last day of the sprint>/`. `--out` overrides the whole path. |
| `markdown` | `true` | Also write `review.md`. |
| `pptx` | `false` | Also write `deck.pptx`, an editable PowerPoint with speaker notes. Needs `pptxgenjs` installed (`npm i -D pptxgenjs`). `--pptx` does the same for one run. |

Every run also adds a line to `<dir>/costs.csv`: the dates, the models that answered, the tokens and the estimated cost in US dollars. The CLI prints the run's cost and the total so far.

---

<!-- docs/screenshots.md -->

# Screenshots

Before and after pictures are what make a sprint review land. sprint-review can add two kinds of pictures:

- **Before and after slides** for screens that changed during the sprint, with one line on what to look at.
- **A screenshot on a theme slide**, when one shows what the theme is about.

There are three ways to get them: from your visual tests, from two folders, or taken by the tool from URLs you choose (best on staging with demo data, so no customer data ends up on a slide). Screenshots are always optional: without them, theme slides show an icon instead and the deck still looks complete.

Which to pick:

| | Works best when | The catch |
|---|---|---|
| `git` | You have visual tests | Only the screens your tests photograph |
| `folder` | You'd rather pick the pictures yourself, or the app is hard to reach from a script | Somebody must remember a *before* picture at the start of the sprint, with the same crop |
| `capture` | The app can be opened from your machine | It needs a login: a saved session, or a test account |

## Option 1: pictures from your visual tests (`git`)

If your project has visual regression tests (Playwright `toHaveScreenshot`, Cypress, Storybook, Chromatic exports…), the reference pictures live in the repository and change in the same commit as the UI. That makes them perfect: real screens, made-up test data, and a history.

```yaml
screenshots:
  source: git
  dir: e2e/__screenshots__/screens.spec.ts
  names:
    dashboard: Dashboard
    customer-page: Customer page
  ignore: { left: 240, top: 64 }
```

How it works:

1. It lists the PNG files under `dir` that changed during the sprint.
2. For each one it takes the version at the start and at the end of the sprint. A picture that only appeared during the sprint uses its first version as "before".
3. It compares them pixel by pixel, skipping `ignore.left` pixels on the left of desktop pictures (a side menu) and `ignore.top` pixels at the top (a top bar). So adding one menu item doesn't mark every screen as changed. Small differences (anti-aliasing, a moving background) stay under the tolerance.
4. On desktop it crops both pictures to where the change is, so the slide shows that part large.
5. The AI writes one line per changed screen on what to look at, or skips it when the change is too small. Only screens with such a line get a slide.

`dir` is a path from the repository root.

## Option 2: two folders (`folder`)

Export or take pictures any way you like, and put them in two folders:

```
screens/
  before/
    dashboard-desktop.png
    customer-page-desktop.png
    customer-page-phone.png
  after/
    dashboard-desktop.png
    customer-page-desktop.png
    customer-page-phone.png
```

```yaml
screenshots:
  source: folder
  before: screens/before
  after: screens/after
```

Pictures that are in both folders and differ are compared exactly as above. Pictures in `after` are also available for theme slides.

## Option 3: the tool takes them (`capture`)

No visual tests? Give sprint-review the pages and it photographs them with Playwright. Each run keeps the pictures in a folder per day; the next review compares the last pictures from before the sprint with the newest ones.

```bash
npm install --save-dev playwright-core   # uses the Chrome you have installed
# or: npm install --save-dev playwright && npx playwright install chromium
```

```yaml
screenshots:
  source: capture
  baseUrl: https://staging.example.com
  pages:
    customer-page: /customers/1042      # screen key: path or full URL
    planner: /planner?branch=north
    planner-progress:                   # one element: a card, a panel, a chart
      url: /planner?branch=north
      selector: "section:has(h2:text-is('Progress'))"
  devices: [desktop, phone]             # default: desktop
  mask: [".email", "[data-private]"]    # painted over before the picture is taken
  storageState: .auth/staging.json      # optional: a logged-in session (see below)
  wait: 800                             # ms after the page settles, default 500
  storage: .sprint-review/screenshots   # default
  names:
    customer-page: Customer page
```

Take today's pictures:

```bash
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review capture
```

You rarely need to: making a review takes today's pictures first when its sprint ends today and there are none yet (`onReview: false` turns that off). Those are this review's *after* and the next review's *before*. If they can't be taken (logged out, the app is down), the review says so and goes on with the pictures there are. Keep the storage folder between runs: commit it, or cache it in CI. The first run has nothing to compare with, so its pictures only show on theme slides.

### Logging in

Two ways, pick one:

- **A saved session** (simplest). Log in once in a browser that saves the session: `npx playwright-core codegen --channel=chrome --save-storage=.auth/staging.json https://staging.example.com/login`, log in, close the window. Point `storageState` at the file and keep it out of git. Capture saves the session back after every run, because apps often hand out a new token on each visit and the old one stops working. It lasts as long as the app keeps a session alive between reviews; when it is gone, capture stops with "Not logged in" and you log in again.
- **A test account** (for CI, or an app that logs you out often). Capture fills in the login form itself. The config names the environment variables that hold the values, never the values. Use an account that can see only demo data. It doesn't work with single sign-on or two-factor login.

```yaml
  login:
    url: /login
    fields:
      "input[type=email]": SCREENSHOT_EMAIL        # names of environment variables
      "input[type=password]": SCREENSHOT_PASSWORD
    submit: "button[type=submit]"
```

When a page sends capture to a login page (`/login`, `/signin`, `/auth`), it stops right away rather than photographing the login page ten times.

- **Components make the best slides.** A selector crops the picture to one card or panel, which reads far better on a slide than a whole page, whose text ends up a few pixels tall. The writer prefers them, and they are taken at twice the sharpness (whole pages at normal sharpness, to keep the deck small) (any Playwright selector works: CSS, `text=`, `:has()`, `xpath=`). A selector that finds nothing is skipped and named in the output.
- **Point it at staging with demo data**, never production. `mask` is a safety net, not a plan.
- **No Playwright browser download?** Set `SPRINT_REVIEW_CHROME` to a Chrome or Chromium binary.

## File names

| File name | Screen key | Device |
|---|---|---|
| `customer-page-desktop.png` | `customer-page` | desktop |
| `customer-page-phone.png` | `customer-page` | phone |
| `customer-page-mobile.png` | `customer-page` | phone |
| `customer-page.png` | `customer-page` | desktop |
| `dashboard-mobile-chromium-linux.png` | `dashboard` | phone (Playwright's browser and platform suffix is dropped) |

The screen key turns into a readable name ("customer-page" → "Customer page") unless you set one in `names`. The order of `names` is also the order of the slides.

Phone pictures are shown upright, in a phone frame.

## Short video clips

A feature you click through shows better moving. Record a few seconds of it with any screen recorder, save it as `.mp4` or `.webm` (8 MB at most, since it goes inside the deck), and name it per screen key:

```yaml
screenshots:
  source: git
  dir: e2e/__screenshots__
  videos:
    planner: docs/clips/planner.mp4
```

A theme showing that screen plays the clip muted in a loop while its slide is open, with the screenshot as its first frame. With reduced motion, in PowerPoint and on paper, the screenshot shows.

## Dark mode

With `brand.theme: dark`, a light screenshot glares on the black slides. If your app has a dark mode, give the deck dark pictures too:

- **Capture:** set `screenshots.darkMode: true` and every page is also photographed in the app's dark mode (Playwright's `colorScheme: dark`). It only works when the app follows the system setting.
- **Git or folders:** add the dark picture next to the light one with `-dark` in the name: `planner-desktop-dark.png`.

The dark deck uses a dark pair when both the before and the after picture have one, and the light pair otherwise, so a comparison never mixes the two (that would count every screen as changed). A light picture on the dark deck is dimmed a little.

## Tips

- **Use made-up data in your test fixtures.** Then the pictures are safe to show anywhere.
- **Set `ignore` to your layout's menu and top bar sizes**, in pixels at the screenshot's resolution.
- **Connect areas to screens** so a theme about an area shows its screen:

```yaml
areas:
  planner: { icon: calendar, label: Workshop planner, screen: planner }
```

<!-- docs/github-action.md -->

# GitHub Action

The action is `guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0`, listed on GitHub Marketplace as [Sprint Review Deck](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/sprint-review-deck).

Run sprint-review on a schedule, so the draft is ready before the meeting.

## Setup

1. Add your Anthropic API key as a repository secret named `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions).
2. Optionally commit a `sprint-review.config.yml` to the repository root.
3. Add a workflow, such as `.github/workflows/sprint-review.yml`.

> **Important:** check out the full history with `fetch-depth: 0`. The default shallow checkout has only the last commit, and the action stops with a clear error when the history doesn't reach back to before the sprint.

## The simplest workflow: an artifact

```yaml
name: Sprint review
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 7 * * 5'   # review day (here Friday) at 07:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch:       # and a button to run it by hand

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0
        id: review
        with:
          anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: sprint-review
          path: ${{ steps.review.outputs.dir }}
```

Download the artifact from the run, open `deck.html`, present. The summary and the check log are also in the run's job summary.

> Every two weeks instead? GitHub's cron has no "every other week". Run weekly and skip odd weeks in a step, or start it by hand with the **Run workflow** button.

## A draft as a pull request

The review becomes a pull request. Reviewing the draft means reviewing the PR; merging it means it's approved. Anyone can fix a word in GitHub's file editor before merging.

```yaml
name: Sprint review
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 7 * * 2'
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0
        id: review
        with:
          anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
      - uses: peter-evans/create-pull-request@v7
        with:
          branch: sprint-review/${{ github.run_id }}
          title: Sprint review draft
          body-path: ${{ steps.review.outputs.markdown }}
          add-paths: sprint-reviews/
          commit-message: 'docs: sprint review draft'
```

After an edit to `review.json` in the PR, rebuild the deck locally with `npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review render <path>/review.json` and push, or add a workflow that does it on push.

## A shareable link with GitHub Pages

Publish the deck so you can share one link:

```yaml
name: Sprint review
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 7 * * 2'
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0
        id: review
        with:
          anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          out: site
      - run: cp site/deck.html site/index.html
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: site
      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
        id: deploy
```

Turn on Pages first: Settings → Pages → Source: **GitHub Actions**. Pages on a public repository are public, so only use this when the deck may be seen by anyone with the link. For a private audience use the artifact or the pull request.

## Inputs

| Input | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `anthropic-api-key` | | Your Anthropic API key, from a secret. Required unless you use OpenAI. |
| `openai-api-key` | | Your OpenAI API key, for `model.provider: openai`. |
| `github-token` | `github.token` | Reads pull request titles and descriptions as context. `''` turns it off. |
| `config` | auto | Path to the config file. |
| `since` | | First day of the sprint, `YYYY-MM-DD`. |
| `until` | today | Last day of the sprint. |
| `from` | | Start at a tag or commit instead of a date. |
| `to` | `HEAD` | End at a tag or commit. |
| `out` | `sprint-reviews/<date>` | Folder to write to. |
| `pptx` | `false` | Also write `deck.pptx`. |
| `slack` | `false` | Post the summary to `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL`. |
| `deck-url` | | Link to the published deck, for the Slack button. |
| `summary` | `true` | Add the review and the check log to the job summary. |
| `version` | `0` | The npm version of `@guuskeunen/sprint-review` to run. `0` means the newest 0.x. |

## Outputs

| Output | Description |
|---|---|
| `dir` | The folder everything was written to. |
| `deck` | Path of `deck.html`. |
| `review` | Path of `review.json`. |
| `markdown` | Path of `review.md`. |
| `checks` | Path of `checks.md`. |
| `pptx` | Path of `deck.pptx`, when `pptx` is on. |

## Reviews per release instead of per sprint

```yaml
on:
  release:
    types: [published]
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - id: previous
        run: echo "tag=$(git describe --tags --abbrev=0 ${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}^)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - uses: guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0
        with:
          anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          from: ${{ steps.previous.outputs.tag }}
          to: ${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}
```

The review then covers exactly what changed since the previous release.

## Other CI systems

The action is a thin wrapper around the CLI. Anywhere with Node 22 and a git history that reaches back to before the sprint:

```bash
npx --yes @guuskeunen/sprint-review generate --json
```

### GitLab CI

A ready-to-copy job, with an optional GitLab Pages job, is in [`examples/gitlab-ci.yml`](../examples/gitlab-ci.yml):

```yaml
sprint-review:
  image: node:22
  variables:
    GIT_DEPTH: 0          # the whole history
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
  script:
    - npx --yes @guuskeunen/sprint-review@0 generate --out sprint-review-deck
  artifacts:
    paths: [sprint-review-deck/]
```

Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as a masked CI/CD variable, and add a pipeline schedule for review day.

## Posting to Slack

Create an [incoming webhook](https://api.slack.com/messaging/webhooks), store it as a secret, and pass `--slack`. The message has the title, the sprint headline and one line per theme, plus a button to the deck when you give its URL:

```yaml
      - uses: guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0
        with:
          anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          slack: true
          deck-url: https://acme.github.io/spoke/sprint-review/
        env:
          SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL }}
```

## Pull request descriptions

In GitHub Actions the action passes the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so pull request titles and descriptions are read automatically (see [`github`](configuration.md#github) in the config). Give the job `pull-requests: read` permission if your repository restricts the token:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: read
```

## Screenshots taken in CI

With `screenshots.source: capture`, run `capture` before `generate` and keep the pictures between runs with a cache:

```yaml
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: .sprint-review/screenshots
          key: sprint-review-shots-${{ github.run_id }}
          restore-keys: sprint-review-shots-
      - run: npm i -D playwright && npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review capture
      - uses: guuskeunen/sprint-review@v0
        with:
          anthropic-api-key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
```

---

<!-- docs/editing.md -->

# Editing and presenting

## Most of the time: just present it

The deck is a draft, but it's written to be presented as it is. Read it through once, glance at `checks.md`, and go.

## Changing the content

### In the editor

Making a review in a terminal opens it in the editor right away. Later, or for an older review:

```bash
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review edit sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/review.json
```

`--no-edit` skips the editor; it never opens in CI or without a terminal. The editor opens a local editor in your browser: the content on the left, the live deck on the right. Every change shows in the deck as you type, before you save. Click into a theme and the preview jumps to its slide. Word counts show the same limits the checks use. **Save and rebuild** (or Ctrl/⌘ + S) writes `review.json` and rebuilds `deck.html` next to it (and `deck.pptx` when `output.pptx` is on). Ctrl+C in the terminal stops the editor.

**Open live view** shows the deck on its own in a new window, for a second screen or a call: it follows every edit as you type and the slide you're working on.

**From the deck:** a deck opened from your disk has an **Edit** button in the top right corner. It opens the editor when it's running; when it isn't, it shows the command that starts it for this deck, ready to copy. Next to it, **Download** gives a PDF (every slide a page, through the print dialog) and the PowerPoint when one was written with the deck (`--pptx`). Published and shared decks show only **Download**, with the deck as one HTML file that works offline too, and the PowerPoint when a `deck.pptx` sits next to the deck.

**Downloading from the editor:** **Download** in the editor's top bar gives a PDF, a PowerPoint and the deck as one HTML file. It saves your edits first, so you get what you see. The PowerPoint is made on the spot, also when the review was written without `--pptx` (it needs `pptxgenjs`, see [PowerPoint](#powerpoint)).

The editor only listens on `127.0.0.1`, and only the page it opened can talk to it. `--port` picks another port (default 4321).

### By hand

Everything on the slides is in `review.json`, next to the deck:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Sprint review November 16, 2026",
  "period": "November 3 to November 16, 2026",
  "headline": "The front desk sees a whole customer on one page",
  "themes": [
    {
      "title": "Customer profile",
      "icon": "users",
      "value": "quality",
      "effect": "Front desk staff see everything a customer bought or had repaired on one page.",
      "layout": "auto",
      "points": ["Purchases, repairs and services sit in one list with their source"],
      "notes": "Open the customer page for Sarah Mitchell and point at the source labels.",
      "screen": null
    }
  ],
  "underTheHood": [{ "text": "Vite is up to date", "kind": "maintenance" }],
  "questions": ["Which repairs would you still type in by hand?"],
  "screens": [],
  "milestones": [{ "text": "Book a repair online", "done": true }],
  "usage": [{ "label": "repairs booked", "value": 312, "previous": 268 }]
}
```

What you can change:

| To… | Edit |
|---|---|
| Fix a word | Any `headline`, `text`, `title`, `effect` (the slide's title), `points`, `notes` or `questions`. |
| Reorder themes | Move items in `themes`. |
| Drop a slide | Remove the theme, the screen from `screens`, or empty `underTheHood`. |
| Change an icon | `icon`, see `sprint-review icons`. |
| Change what a theme brings | `value`: `faster`, `quality`, `less_manual_work`, `less_risk`, `insight`, or `null`. |
| Remove a theme's picture | Set `screen` to `null`. |
| Change a slide's layout | `layout`: `auto`, `split`, `full`, `icon` or `card` (see [design](design.md#theme-layouts)). |
| Label a line under the hood | `kind`: `security`, `reliability`, `speed` or `maintenance`. |
| Fix a number | `usage`. |

Then rebuild:

```bash
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review render sprint-reviews/2026-11-16/review.json
```

`render` also picks up config changes: a new logo, color, goal or labels show up in old reviews when you render them again.

## PowerPoint

Some teams present from PowerPoint or Keynote, or want to add a slide by hand. Add `--pptx` (or set `output.pptx: true`) and `deck.pptx` is written next to the deck: the same slides, editable, with the speaker notes in the notes pane. It needs `pptxgenjs` (`npm i -D pptxgenjs`). `render` and the editor rebuild it too when `output.pptx` is on.

`npm audit` may then report `image-size`: `pptxgenjs` lists it as a dependency but never calls it, so the advisory doesn't reach sprint-review, and only a `pptxgenjs` release can remove it. To clear the report, add this to your `package.json`:

```json
"overrides": { "image-size": "^2.1.0" }
```

The HTML deck stays the richer one: animations, the presenter window and before-and-after wipes don't exist in PowerPoint.

## Presenting

Open `deck.html` in any browser. It has no outside dependencies, so it also works offline and from a USB stick.

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| → ↓ Space Enter PageDown | Next slide |
| ← ↑ Backspace PageUp | Previous slide |
| Home / End | First / last slide |
| F | Full screen |
| P | Presenter window: speaker notes, the next slide's title and a timer, for your own screen |
| N | Show the speaker notes at the bottom of this window |

Click the right two thirds of the screen to go forward, the left third to go back. Swipe on a phone or tablet. The address ends in `#3` on slide 3, so a link can open on a specific slide.

The animations respect your system's *reduce motion* setting.

## Exporting to PDF

Print the deck (Cmd/Ctrl + P) and choose **Save as PDF**. Every slide becomes one 16:9 page, without animations or controls. Turn on **Background graphics** in the print dialog to keep the colors.

## Sharing

- **Send the file.** `deck.html` is one file, usually a few hundred kilobytes with screenshots.
- **Host it.** Any static host works: GitHub Pages (see [the GitHub Action guide](github-action.md#a-shareable-link-with-github-pages)), Netlify, S3, an intranet.
- **Paste the summary.** `review.md` is ready for a pull request, Slack or an email.

---

<!-- docs/design.md -->

# How the deck is designed

The deck follows rules from presentation research: Apple's keynotes and Human Interface Guidelines, Nancy Duarte's *slide:ology* and glance test, Garr Reynolds' *Presentation Zen*, Michael Alley's assertion-evidence slides, and sprint review practice (the Scrum Guide, Roman Pichler, Mountain Goat, Linear's changelog). A test measures most of these rules in a real browser (`test/deck/layout.test.ts`), so a change that breaks one fails CI.

## Rules the deck keeps

| Rule | Where it comes from | How the deck keeps it |
|---|---|---|
| One message per slide, stated in the title as a full sentence | Alley, Duarte | A theme's title is what a user can do now, in 12 words at most; the theme's name sits small above it. A title that joins two messages with a semicolon gets a warning. |
| Readable at a glance: about 40 words besides the title | Duarte's glance test | The writer is asked for two to four points (depending on `deck.density`). A slide over the budget gets a warning in the check log. The text is never shrunk to fit. |
| Four text sizes for the whole deck | Butterick, Apple | 120, 64, 36 and 24 px at 1920 x 1080. They scale with the window. |
| Nothing under 24 px; body text 36 px | Apple tvOS, Alley | The smallest text is 24 px: labels, captions, the cards' sentences. |
| Margins of at least 96 px | Apple, Duarte | 154 px left and right, 97 px top. |
| Evidence over text | Alley, Reynolds | A screenshot takes most of a theme slide, but only one that shows the theme's change: a picture of something nearby is worse than the icon, which is then shown at hero size. Close-ups of one card or panel are preferred over whole pages, whose text is too small on a slide. |
| Screenshots cropped, with no device frame unless the device is the point | Reynolds, documentation style guides | Rounded corners of 10 px and a soft shadow (a hairline border and slight dimming in the dark theme). A phone frame appears only for a theme about the phone. |
| Before and after: the same crop and size, labeled | Alley | Both pictures share one size and crop. The title says what changed. |
| One brand color becomes the whole palette, every color measured | Radix, Material, WCAG | Grays and lines take a little of the brand's hue; body text is at least 4.5:1, labels and the accent at least 3:1, in both themes (`src/deck/colors.ts`). |
| Motion only to show what arrives or changed | NN/g, Tversky et al. | Every animation runs once, in 400 ms or less. The frame around a change appears after the after picture is in. |
| No logo or chrome on every slide | Reynolds | The logo appears on the cover and the closing slide only. |
| The same slide type looks the same every time; the deck still has rhythm | Duarte, Pitch, Keynote masters | The title always sits in the same place. A screenshot layout used twice in a row is mirrored the second time. |

## The story

1. **Cover**: the product's name, "Sprint review" and the period (the date isn't repeated in the title), the sprint goal when `goal` is set, and the sprint's strongest screenshot running off the right edge.
2. **The sprint headline**: the one change that matters most to a user, in at most ten plain words (never two things joined with "and", never how it works), and a row with the theme names. A sprint goal is set before the sprint and can't be read from git, so the headline describes what was done.
3. **Last sprint**: what the previous review showed as next on the roadmap, and whether it is done now. Only when there is a previous review in the output folder and a roadmap; the audience checks promises before hearing new ones (GitLab publishes its kickoff and retrospective as a pair for the same reason).
4. **You asked**: requests from `FEEDBACK.md` that this sprint answered, each with what was done, backed by a commit.
5. **Theme slides**: the biggest themes, one slide each. `deck.density` sets how many: 2, 3 or 4.
6. **More changes**: the remaining themes as cards, one message each, across the slide's width. Their points go into the speaker notes.
7. **Before and after**: one slide per changed screen, the change framed. When it is small, one press of → zooms into it (Tversky et al.: animation helps most for moving from overview to detail) and the next moves on.
8. **Also shipped**: work behind the scenes, with a label per line (security, reliability, speed, maintenance).
9. **Roadmap**: how many milestones are reached, as a line through the last ones reached and the next ones.
10. **Numbers**: one big number per idea, at most four.
11. **Questions**: two or three specific questions for the audience, in place of a bare "Questions?" slide.

The audience sets the defaults: executives get a brief deck with the numbers right after the headline and no slide about work behind the scenes, the team gets a detailed deck, everyone else a standard one. `deck.density`, `deck.order` and `deck.sections` change that.

## Theme layouts

The deck picks a layout from what a theme has. You can override it per theme in the editor or in `review.json` (`"layout"`):

| Layout | When | |
|---|---|---|
| `split` | The theme has a desktop screenshot | Points beside the picture. |
| `full` | The screenshot is at least 2.4 times as wide as it is tall (a row of cards), or chosen by hand | The screenshot fills the slide's width, with the points in a row below it. Beside the points a strip would shrink to a thin band. |
| `phone` | The screenshot is a phone screen | Points beside an upright phone. |
| `icon` | No screenshot | The icon at hero size beside the points. |
| `card` | Chosen by hand | The theme goes on the shared *More changes* slide. |
| `auto` | The default | The deck decides. |

The HTML deck, the PowerPoint file and the editor all follow one plan (`src/deck/plan.ts`), so they show the same slides in the same order.

<!-- docs/integrations.md -->

# Integrations

sprint-review is a command-line tool first. Everything else here builds on it.

## The Claude Code plugin

The skill and the MCP server in one install:

```
/plugin marketplace add guuskeunen/sprint-review
/plugin install sprint-review@sprint-review
```

Then ask Claude Code for a sprint review, or type `/sprint-review`. The plugin runs `npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review@0 mcp`, so it picks up new releases by itself. Set your API key in the environment Claude Code starts from.

## Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP clients

`sprint-review mcp` runs an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server over stdio. An AI assistant in your editor can then check the setup, preview a sprint's commits, write the review and rebuild it after an edit, and tell you what the checks did.

**Claude Code**

```bash
claude mcp add sprint-review -- npx -y @guuskeunen/sprint-review mcp
```

**Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Desktop and others** (their MCP config file):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sprint-review": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@guuskeunen/sprint-review", "mcp"],
      "env": { "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY": "sk-ant-..." }
    }
  }
}
```

**As a bundle:** every [release](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/releases/latest) has `sprint-review.mcpb` attached. Open it in Claude Desktop (or another client that installs MCP bundles) to install the server with a form for your API key. The bundle starts that release's npm package, so Node 22 or newer must be installed. The server is also in the [MCP registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) as `io.github.guuskeunen/sprint-review`, and listed on [mcpservers.org](https://mcpservers.org/servers/guuskeunen/sprint-review).

Then ask: *"Make our sprint review for the last two weeks"*, or *"What would the sprint review read for v1.4.0 to v1.5.0?"*.

| Tool | Does | Changes files |
|---|---|---|
| `check_sprint_review_setup` | Runs the same checks as `doctor`. | No |
| `preview_sprint_commits` | Lists the commits for a range, without a model call. | No |
| `generate_sprint_review` | Writes the deck and returns the paths, the themes, every check and the cost. Replaces an earlier deck in the same folder. | Yes |
| `render_sprint_review` | Rebuilds the deck from an edited `review.json`. | Yes, the deck only |

Every tool takes `directory` (the project folder; default where the server started). `preview_sprint_commits` and `generate_sprint_review` also take the range arguments `since`, `until`, `from` and `to`. Each tool tells the client whether it only reads, changes files or calls outside services (MCP tool annotations), so clients can ask before the ones that do.

## The Claude Code skill on its own

[`plugin/skills/sprint-review/SKILL.md`](../plugin/skills/sprint-review/SKILL.md) teaches Claude Code the workflow: check, preview, generate, report the checks, edit. The plugin includes it; without the plugin, copy the folder into your project's `.claude/skills/` (or `~/.claude/skills/` for all projects).

[`plugin/`](../plugin/) is the same skill as a plugin of its own, without the MCP server: that is the version for Anthropic's plugin directory, which takes plugins with a local MCP server, a `package.json` or scripts only from verified organizations. It uses the `sprint-review` command, so install the tool first. The plugin at the repository root has the skill and the MCP server.

## Pull request descriptions

Commit subjects say *what*; pull requests often say *why*. With `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` set, the title and description of the pull request behind each commit go to the writer as extra context. In GitHub Actions this is on by default. Locally:

```bash
GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review
```

See [`github`](configuration.md#github) for the options. Pull request text is treated as untrusted input, like commit messages: wrapped and marked as data in the prompt.

## Other models

Claude by default; Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini, Mistral, and local models with Ollama or LM Studio are a config line away. See [models and providers](models.md) for setup and an honest table of what's been tested.

## Slack

```bash
export SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.slack.com/services/...
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review --slack --deck-url https://acme.github.io/spoke/review/
```

Or `slack: true` in the config. See [posting to Slack from CI](github-action.md#posting-to-slack).

## GitLab, Bitbucket, Jenkins…

Anywhere with Node 22 and a git history that reaches back to before the sprint: `npx --yes @guuskeunen/sprint-review generate --json`. A GitLab job is in [`examples/gitlab-ci.yml`](../examples/gitlab-ci.yml).

## As a library

All of it is importable from TypeScript or JavaScript. See [the library guide](library.md).

<!-- docs/models.md -->

# Models and providers

sprint-review works with any model that can answer in a fixed JSON shape. Claude is the default because it writes the best slides; the others are there for choice, cost and privacy.

## Which to pick

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Best slides, simplest setup | `anthropic` (default), Claude Opus with Sonnet as fallback |
| Your company already has Claude through AWS | `bedrock` |
| Your company already has Azure OpenAI | `azure` |
| One key for many models, or comparing them | `openrouter` |
| Nothing may leave your network | `ollama` or `lmstudio` |

## Tested models

What "tested" means here, honestly:

- **Verified:** run end to end against the real service with this version.
- **Code tested:** the request and answer handling are covered by the test suite against recorded or fake responses, but not yet run against the live service. These should work; please [report how it went](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/issues/new?title=Model%20report:%20).

| Provider | Model | Status | Quality of the slides |
|---|---|---|---|
| `anthropic` | `claude-opus-5-5` | The default. Verified: benchmark 100/100, live runs on 80 and 294 commits | Best: clear themes, good effect sentences. About $0.30 a review |
| `anthropic` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` | The fallback. Verified: benchmark 100/100, live runs on 80 and 294 commits | Very good. About $0.20 a review |
| `bedrock` | Claude through Bedrock | Code tested; request signing checked against AWS's official test vector | Same as Claude directly |
| `openai` | `gpt-6.2-sol` | Verified: benchmark 97/100, live runs on 80 and 294 commits (in JSON mode: it takes no tools with reasoning on Chat Completions) | Very good |
| `openai` | `gpt-5.4-mini` | Verified: benchmark 87/100, live runs | Plainer: fewer themes, more lines the reader flags. Fast |
| `openai`, `azure` | Other GPT models | Code tested | Expected good |
| `openrouter` | Any | Code tested | Depends on the model |
| `gemini` | `gemini-3.6-flash` | Verified: benchmark 100/100, live runs on 80 and 294 commits | Good, and the cheapest: about $0.02 a review. Thinner on long ranges |
| `gemini` | Other Gemini models | Code tested | Expected good |
| `mistral` | Mistral models | Code tested | Expected decent |
| `ollama`, `lmstudio` | Qwen, Llama, Mistral and others, 30B+ recommended | Code tested | Works, but plainer: fewer and flatter themes |

Whatever the model, every answer goes through the same checks: a point that can't be traced to a real commit is dropped, word limits hold, tooling goes under the hood. A weaker model gives a plainer deck, not a wrong one.

Tried a model? Open an issue with the provider, model and how the deck read, and it goes in this table.

## Setup per provider

Keys always come from environment variables, never from the config.

### Anthropic (default)

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
```

No config needed. To pick another model: `model: { name: claude-sonnet-5-5 }`.

### Amazon Bedrock

```yaml
model:
  provider: bedrock
  name: us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5-v1:0   # your model or inference profile id, from the Bedrock console
  region: eu-central-1                      # or set AWS_REGION
```

Credentials, one of:

- a **Bedrock API key**: `export AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK=...` (simplest; create one in the Bedrock console)
- **AWS access keys**: `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and, for temporary credentials, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`. This is what `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` sets in GitHub Actions, so OIDC roles work.

Your account needs access to the model in that region (Bedrock console → Model access).

### OpenAI

```yaml
model: { provider: openai, name: gpt-5.1 }
```

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
```

### Azure OpenAI

```yaml
model:
  provider: azure
  name: my-deployment                                   # your deployment name
  baseUrl: https://my-resource.openai.azure.com/openai/v1
```

```bash
export AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY=...
```

### OpenRouter

```yaml
model: { provider: openrouter, name: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 }
```

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
```

### Google Gemini

```yaml
model: { provider: gemini, name: gemini-3.6-flash }
```

Gemini is asked to think at low effort: its thinking counts against `maxTokens`, and at its default effort it could use up the room before it wrote the slides.

```bash
export GEMINI_API_KEY=...
```

### Mistral

```yaml
model: { provider: mistral, name: mistral-large-latest }
```

```bash
export MISTRAL_API_KEY=...
```

### Ollama (local)

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:32b
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 ollama serve     # a large context window matters
```

```yaml
model: { provider: ollama, name: "qwen3:32b" }
```

No key needed. Run `sprint-review doctor` to check that Ollama answers and the model is there.

### LM Studio (local)

Load a model, start the server (Developer tab), then:

```yaml
model: { provider: lmstudio, name: qwen3-32b }
```

### Any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint

A gateway, vLLM, LiteLLM, Groq, Together, DeepSeek…

```yaml
model:
  provider: openai
  name: the-model
  baseUrl: https://my-gateway.example.com/v1
```

## Settings for smaller and local models

| Setting | What it does |
|---|---|
| `model.mode: json` | Ask for JSON matching the schema instead of forcing a tool call. The default for Ollama and LM Studio; try it for any server whose tool calling is unreliable. |
| `model.maxInputChars` | How much of the commit log the model gets. Default 120,000 characters, 24,000 for local models. A longer sprint is fitted to it, every product commit first; `checks.md` counts what was left out. |
| `model.maxTokens` | Room for the answer, thinking included. Default 16,000. |
| `model.fallback` | A second model when the first fails. Default Sonnet for Anthropic, none for others. |

If a model answers in text instead of through the tool, sprint-review looks for the JSON in its answer and checks it like any other. Local models are slow: a run can take several minutes.
