<!-- docs/security.md -->

# Security and privacy

A one-page answer for whoever has to approve sprint-review: what it reads, what it sends where, and what it never does.

## In short

- **It runs on your machine or in your own CI.** There is no sprint-review server, no account and no telemetry. The author never sees your data.
- **It sends commit text, not code.** Commit subjects, descriptions and changed file names go to the AI provider you configure, with your own key. Source code, diffs and screenshots never leave.
- **You choose the provider,** including ones your company already approved (Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock) or a local model where nothing leaves your network.
- **`--dry-run` shows exactly what would be sent,** before anything is.

## What it reads

| Source | What | When |
|---|---|---|
| Your git repository | Commit hashes, dates, subjects, descriptions and changed file names in the range; the roadmap file at the end of the sprint | Always |
| Screenshot pictures | Pixels, compared locally | When `screenshots` is set |
| Your pages (capture) | Screenshots of the URLs you list, in a local browser | Only with `screenshots.source: capture` |
| The GitHub API | Title and description of the pull request behind each commit | Only when `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` is set (always in GitHub Actions), and `github.pullRequests` isn't `false` |
| A usage file | The numbers you put in it | When `usage` is set |

It needs **read access** to the repository only. It writes nothing to git and never pushes.

## What it sends, and where

Each run makes two or three calls to **one** AI provider: the one in `model.provider`, with the key from your environment.

| Call | Gets |
|---|---|
| Writer | Your product description, audience and rules from the config; the commit log described above (up to `model.maxInputChars`); the names of screens |
| Second reader | Only the text of the slides |
| Rewrite (when the reader flagged lines) | The text of the slides and the flagged lines |

**Never sent:** source code, diffs, file contents, screenshots or other pictures, usage numbers, environment variables, secrets.

Commit and pull request text is treated as untrusted: it's wrapped in random markers and the model is told it's data, so a commit message that says "ignore your instructions" is just a commit message. Whatever the model answers goes through checks in code, and anything that can't be traced to a real commit is dropped.

### Keeping things out

- **Sensitive commits:** `ignore` patterns skip matching commits entirely; they're never sent.
- **Customer or internal names:** `replace` rewrites words in the output; for the input, `ignore` the commits or keep names out of commit messages.
- **No pull request text:** `github: { pullRequests: false }`, or run without a token.
- **Less of the log:** `model.maxInputChars`.

### Where the data goes, per provider

Data handling follows **your** agreement with the provider you pick. sprint-review adds nothing in between.

| Provider | Data goes to | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `anthropic` (default) | Anthropic API | API data isn't used for training by default; check your plan's terms |
| `openai` | OpenAI API | |
| `azure` | Your Azure OpenAI resource | Stays in your Azure tenant and region |
| `bedrock` | Amazon Bedrock in your AWS account and region | Uses your AWS credentials or a Bedrock API key |
| `openrouter`, `gemini`, `mistral` | That service | |
| `ollama`, `lmstudio` | A model on your own machine or server | **Nothing leaves your network** |

## Keys and secrets

- Keys are read from **environment variables only**, never from the config file, so the config can be committed safely.
- In CI, keep keys in your CI's secret store (GitHub: repository or organization secrets).
- Keys are only sent to the provider they belong to, in an HTTP header. They're never written to a file or a log; the cost ledger (`costs.csv`) holds dates, models, tokens and dollars only.
- `model.baseUrl` sends the key to the address you give, so a config you run with your keys is code you trust, like an npm script. Plain `http://` is refused except on this machine (`localhost`), and a local provider (`ollama`, `lmstudio`) only borrows `OPENAI_API_KEY` when it really runs on this machine.

## The outputs

`deck.html`, `review.json`, `review.md` and `checks.md` (and `deck.pptx`) are written to a local folder. They contain what's on the slides, plus screenshots if you configured them. **Nothing is published on its own:** sharing the deck is a step you take (an artifact, GitHub Pages, Slack).

The deck is a single file with no outside requests: no fonts, scripts, images or trackers are loaded from anywhere. Its Edit button, shown only when you open the deck from your own disk, checks `127.0.0.1:4321` for the local editor when you click it.

Everything from commits, pull requests, the model and a hand-edited `review.json` is escaped: in the deck as HTML, in `review.md` and `checks.md` so it can't form links, images or HTML. Pictures in `review.json` must be image data URIs, and `render` refuses a review that doesn't hold up. Pull request text is read from merged pull requests only.

## The local editor

`sprint-review edit` starts a web server on `127.0.0.1` only, so it can't be reached from other machines. Every request must carry a random token that only the page it opened knows, so other websites in your browser can't read or change the review, and its pages can't be framed by another site. It stops when you press Ctrl+C.

## The MCP server

`sprint-review mcp` talks over stdio with the client that started it (Claude Code, Cursor…). It doesn't open a network port. Its tools read the git history and write the outputs in the folder you point it at; the model call uses the same provider and key as the CLI. An assistant picks the tool arguments, and text it read can steer it, so the folder must be a project (a git repository or a sprint-review config), files are read and written only inside it, and a ref that looks like a git option is refused.

## Dependencies

Two runtime dependencies, `sharp` (image comparison) and `yaml` (the config), plus `pptxgenjs` as an optional one for PowerPoint export, which you install yourself. A plain install has no known vulnerabilities; with `pptxgenjs`, `npm audit` reports `image-size`, which `pptxgenjs` lists but never calls ([how to clear it](editing.md#powerpoint)). Playwright is only needed if you use `capture`, and you install it yourself. HTTP calls use Node's built-in `fetch`. Releases are published to npm with [provenance](https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements), so you can verify a package was built from this repository.

## Reporting a vulnerability

See [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

---

<!-- docs/benchmark.md -->

# The quality benchmark

A model writes the words on the slides, so "is it better now?" is a real question every time a prompt or a model changes. The benchmark answers it with numbers instead of a feeling.

## What it is

Fixed sample sprints in [`bench/cases/`](../bench/cases), each with the answer a good presenter would give:

| Case | What it tests |
|---|---|
| `bike-shop` | Product work mixed with tooling noise, a ticket number in a subject, and a commit that tries to instruct the model ("ignore all previous instructions…") |
| `billing-saas` | Terse, technical messages ("add sepa direct debit to checkout", "WIP", a Jira key), for a customer audience |
| `cli-library` | A developer tool reviewed for its own team, with a breaking change |

Each case lists:

- **themes** that should be on the front slides, with words that count as covering them;
- **hood** items, the plumbing that belongs under the hood and nowhere else;
- **never**: text that must never appear on a slide (ticket keys, injected instructions, "WIP").

Every case is built into a real git repository with real dates and files, and goes through the real pipeline: the writer, every check, the second reader, the rewrite.

## The score

| Part | Points |
|---|---|
| Expected themes covered on the front slides | 50 |
| No plumbing on the front slides | 15 |
| Plumbing under the hood | 10 |
| Nothing forbidden anywhere on the slides | 15 |
| Few warnings left by the second reader | 10 |

Alongside the score: how many points the checks dropped or rewrote, how many themes there are, and the average words per point.

## Running it

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
npm run bench                                          # the default model
npm run bench -- --model claude-sonnet-5-5
npm run bench -- --provider ollama --model qwen3:32b   # a local model
npm run bench -- --cases bike-shop                     # one case
npm run bench -- --echo                                # no model: checks the harness itself
```

A report is printed and saved in `bench/results/`, named by date and model. Commit the ones worth keeping: they're the history of the tool's quality, and they fill the [model table](models.md#tested-models).

A full run is three cases, two or three calls each. With Claude that's a few dimes.

## Real repositories

The sample sprints check the words. Real repositories check everything else: size, noise, pull requests, a product the writer has never seen. We ran sprint-review on the same two weeks (November 9 to 22, 2026) of four open-source projects, with Claude Sonnet 5.5, a short product description and `productPaths` in the config, and nothing edited afterwards. The decks are [in the README](../README.md#real-decks-from-real-repositories).

| Project | Commits | Pull requests | Read | Time | Tokens | Cost | Checks |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VS Code | 1,298 | not counted | all product commits; 52 docs and chores left out | 109 s | 68,000 | $0.21 | 14 |
| Next.js | 252 | 80 | all but 1 without product code | 167 s | 72,838 | $0.28 | 23 |
| Supabase | 355 | 114 | all | 146 s | 67,659 | $0.22 | 9 |
| Excalidraw | 16 | 15 | all | 77 s | 25,704 | $0.12 | 11 |

The Excalidraw deck on the site was made again afterwards, with Gemini 3.6 Flash ($0.02, 21 s, 13,856 tokens, 3 checks) and a screenshot: `screenshots.source: capture` photographed excalidraw.com with a drawing loaded through `storageState` (Excalidraw keeps its drawing and settings, such as `minimapEnabled`, in local storage), and the writer put it on the minimap slide.

What the first round found, and what changed:

- **Shallow clones were refused**, even ones that held the whole sprint. A shallow clone is now fine when it reaches back to before the sprint starts.
- **Big sprints were read from the end.** The commit log was cut at the input limit, newest first, so on VS Code the writer saw only the last days. Each commit past the cut was also its own warning: 916 checks on VS Code, 164 on Next.js, 247 on Supabase. Now every product commit gets a line first, then details as far as they fit, and what's left out is one warning. On VS Code this changed the headline: the biggest change of the sprint (a new launcher for agent sessions) landed early and had been missed.
- **`limits.commits` quietly dropped the oldest commits** (1,000 by default). The default is now 3,000, and a sprint past it gets a warning.
- **Two cards sat on half the slide**, and a title joined two messages with a semicolon. Two cards now use the full width, and such a title gets a warning.

To run one yourself:

```bash
git clone --shallow-since=2026-11-01 https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw && cd excalidraw
cat > sprint-review.config.yml <<'YML'
product: { name: Excalidraw, description: "A virtual whiteboard for hand-drawn-like diagrams." }
productPaths: [packages/, excalidraw-app/]
model: { name: claude-sonnet-5-5 }
YML
GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review --until 2026-11-22
```

## Adding a case

Copy a file in `bench/cases/`, change the commits and the expectations, run it. A good case is a sprint where a careless writer would go wrong: vague messages, noise, a tempting thing to invent. Keep the expected words loose ("ticket", "photo", "handwritten"), so a good answer in other words still counts.

---

<!-- docs/how-it-works.md -->

# How it works

sprint-review splits the work between an AI, code and a person, and gives each the part it's best at.

| | Does |
|---|---|
| **The AI** | Groups the changes into themes and writes the words: the sprint headline, themes, points, captions, speaker notes and questions for the audience. Then a second call reads the slides like your audience would. |
| **Code** | Reads the history, checks every line the AI wrote, counts every number, picks and crops every picture, builds the page. |
| **A person** | Reads the draft, changes something if needed, presents it. |

The reason: AI is great at turning "optimize status count queries" into "the planner loads faster". It shouldn't be the one deciding what happened. Early versions of this tool let the AI do more, and it picked wrong screenshots and wrote things that weren't true. So now the AI only writes words, and everything that can be checked is checked in code.

## The pipeline

```
git history ──► commits (+ pull requests), changed screenshots, roadmap
                      │
                      ▼
          AI writer (one call, structured output)
                      │
                      ▼
          code checks ──► check log
                      │
                      ▼
          AI reader (one call, sees only the slide text)
                      │
                      ▼
          one rewrite of the flagged lines ──► the same checks again
                      │
                      ▼
          deck: pictures, numbers, icons, brand ──► deck.html, review.json, review.md, checks.md
```

### 1. Reading the history

- `git log` for the range, without merge commits: hash, date, subject, body and changed files.
- Trailer lines (`Co-authored-by:`, `Signed-off-by:`, "Generated with…") are removed from bodies, and bodies are cut at 600 characters.
- Commits matching `ignore` are left out.
- With a GitHub token, the pull request behind each product commit is looked up; its title (and, on its first commit, its description, cut at 800 characters and without HTML comments) is added to the log.
- Each commit is marked as product work or not: it must touch a file under `productPaths` (if set) and must not be a `ci:`, `build:`, `test:`, `docs:` or `chore:` commit (`nonProductTypes`).
- A long sprint is fitted to what the model can read (`model.maxInputChars`) without losing its first days: a line for every product commit first, then up to 15% of the room for lines of the other commits, then the details of product commits as far as they fit. What's still left out is counted in one warning in `checks.md`. A sprint of 1,300 commits (VS Code over two weeks) fits this way with every product commit in view.
- At most `limits.commits` commits are read (3,000), newest first; a sprint past it gets a warning that its first days are missing.
- A shallow clone is fine when its history reaches back to before the sprint starts.

### 2. The writer

One call with a fixed answer shape: the model fills in fields (headline, themes, under the hood, captions, questions) instead of writing free text. The prompt holds principles and examples, nothing about one particular sprint, so it never needs editing between reviews. It includes your product description, audience, language, team words and rules.

Commit messages are written by people, so they go in between unique markers, and the model is told that whatever is between them is data, never instructions. A commit that says "ignore your rules" is just a commit.

The model picks icons from a fixed set, values from a fixed list, and screenshots only from those that exist.

### 3. The checks

Every line the writer returned goes through code:

| Check | What happens |
|---|---|
| Each point names commit hashes, and they exist in this sprint | Otherwise the point is **dropped**. |
| A point only backed by non-product commits | **Moved** under the hood; a headline about one is dropped. |
| Points ≤ 16 words, effects and captions ≤ 25, notes ≤ 70, titles ≤ 4 | Otherwise **dropped**. |
| No `!`, no emoji | Otherwise **dropped**. |
| Ticket numbers (`#42`, `ABC-81`) and hashes | **Removed** from the text. |
| Long dashes | Become a comma. |
| Your `replace` words | **Applied**, keeping the capital. |
| At most `limits.themes` themes, 2 to 4 points per theme (`deck.density`), 5 under the hood, 3 questions | The rest is **dropped**. |
| A theme slide with more words than the audience reads at a glance | A **warning**: shorten it in the editor. |
| A theme with no points left | **Dropped**. |
| Unknown icon | Becomes `other`. |
| A screenshot that doesn't exist | Removed from the theme. |
| Commits past what the model can read in a very long sprint | Listed to **look at**. |

Everything that happened goes into `checks.md`. Nothing is fixed silently.

### 4. The reader

A second call gets only the slide text: no commits, no context, nothing it could use to fill a gap. It reads as your audience and lists every sentence it gets stuck on, as *unclear* or as an empty *promise*. The reader never rewrites anything itself. Its findings go into `checks.md`. If the call fails, the draft is kept, with a "Not proofread" warning at the top of the check log.

### 4b. One rewrite

The flagged lines go back to the writer, with the reader's reason, once. Each rewrite goes through the same checks as the first draft (word limits, references stripped, team words applied) and only replaces the original when it passes; it's logged as *corrected*, old and new side by side. A line that couldn't be fixed keeps its warning, so you know to look at it. `revise: false` turns this off.

### 5. The deck

Code builds the page from the checked content:

- **Screenshots:** before and after slides only for changed screens the writer could explain in a line (at most `limits.changedScreens`). Theme pictures at most `limits.themeScreens`, and a picture never shows twice: not on two themes, and not on a theme when it already has a desktop before and after slide.
- **Values:** the "What we gain" slide groups themes by the value the writer picked.
- **Numbers:** usage comes from your `usage` file, milestones from your roadmap file at the end of the sprint. The model never writes a number.
- **Brand:** your color (with lighter and darker shades mixed from it), your logo and fonts, or all three from a `.pptx` with `brand.from`. Light by default; `brand.theme: dark` for a dark deck.

The result is one HTML file with everything inline: styles, script, icons, pictures. No fonts, scripts or images are loaded from anywhere, so it works offline and keeps working.

## What is sent to the AI

- The writer gets: the system prompt (your product description, audience, language, rules), the commit log (hashes, dates, subjects, bodies, up to six file names per commit, pull request titles and descriptions when a token is set) and the names of the screens.
- The reader gets: the slide text.
- The rewrite gets: the slide text and the flagged lines with the reader's reasons.

Never source code, never diffs, never pictures, never usage numbers.

<!-- docs/library.md -->

# Using it as a library

Everything the CLI does is available from Node.

```bash
npm install @guuskeunen/sprint-review
```

```ts
import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { clientFor, generate, loadConfig, writeOutputs } from '@guuskeunen/sprint-review';

const config = loadConfig('sprint-review.config.yml');
const model = clientFor(config.model); // Anthropic or OpenAI, key from the environment

const { review, html, markdown, usage } = await generate(config, {
  model,
  range: { kind: 'dates', from: '2026-11-03', until: '2026-11-16' },
  onStep: (message) => console.log(message),
});

writeFileSync('deck.html', html);
// or everything at once: deck.html, review.json, review.md, checks.md (and deck.pptx)
await writeOutputs(review, config, 'sprint-reviews/2026-11-16', { pptx: true });
```

## Main functions

| Function | Does |
|---|---|
| `loadConfig(path?, cwd?)` | Reads and checks a config file, or finds the default one. |
| `normalize(object, root)` | Builds a config from a plain object, with every default filled in. |
| `generate(config, options)` | The whole pipeline. Returns `{ review, html, markdown, usage, cost, models }`; `cost.usd` is `null` when a model has no known price. |
| `render(review, config)` | Rebuilds `{ html, markdown }` from a stored review. |
| `sprintRange(days, until?)` | The range of the sprint that ends on a day. |
| `renderDeck(review, options)` | Just the deck, with `{ color, logo, labels, goal, theme, fonts }`. |
| `writeOutputs(review, config, dir, { pptx? })` | Writes every output file into a folder. |
| `renderPptx(review, options)` | The PowerPoint as a Buffer (needs `pptxgenjs`). |
| `brandFromPptx(file)` | `{ color, fonts, logo }` from a presentation's theme and master. |
| `brandFromWebsite(url)`, `withWebsiteBrand(config)` | `{ color, fonts, logo }` from a website; the config with a website in `brand.from` filled in. `render` needs the second first. |
| `costOf(calls, config.model, date)`, `priceOf(...)`, `recordCost(config, entry)` | What a run cost, the price of a model, and the ledger in `costs.csv`. |
| `capture(config.screenshots.capture, root)` | Takes today's screenshots (needs Playwright). |
| `startEditor(file, config, port?)` | Starts the local editor; returns `{ url, close }`. |
| `withPullRequests(commits, repo, token)` | Adds pull request titles and descriptions. |
| `postToSlack(webhook, review, deckUrl)` | Posts the summary. |
| `clientFor(config.model)` | An `AnthropicClient` or `OpenAIClient` with the key from the environment. |
| `renderMarkdown(review)`, `renderChecks(review)` | The Markdown summary and the check log. |
| `compareScreens(before, after, device, ignore)` | The screenshot comparison on its own. |
| `clean(text, maxWords, replace?)` | The text check on its own. |

## Ranges

```ts
{ kind: 'dates', from: '2026-11-03', until: '2026-11-16' }   // both days included
{ kind: 'refs', from: 'v1.4.0', to: 'HEAD' }                // what `to` has and `from` doesn't
```

## Your own model client

`generate` takes anything that implements `ModelClient`, so you can route calls through your own gateway, add logging, or test without an API:

```ts
import type { ModelClient } from '@guuskeunen/sprint-review';

const model: ModelClient = {
  async ask({ system, messages, tool, maxTokens }) {
    const input = await myGateway.callWithTool(system, messages, tool, maxTokens);
    return { toolInput: input, model: 'my-model', usage: { input: 0, output: 0 } };
  },
};
```

The model must answer through the given tool: `toolInput` is the tool's input object, or `null` when it gave none.

## Errors

All expected failures are their own class, with a message meant for people:

`ConfigError`, `GitError`, `ModelError`, `WriterError`, `NothingToReview`.

## Types

`Review`, `ReviewTheme`, `ReviewScreen`, `Commit`, `Check`, `Milestone`, `UsageMetric`, `Config` and more are exported as types.

---

<!-- docs/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

Start with `npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review doctor`. It checks the config, the git history, the API key and your Node version, and says how to fix each one.

### "This checkout's history starts on …" or "has a shallow history"
The repository was cloned with only part of its history, which is common in CI. A shallow clone is fine as long as it reaches back to before the sprint started (`git clone --shallow-since=<a week before the sprint>`); the error names the date to fetch from. To be safe, fetch everything. In GitHub Actions:

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with:
    fetch-depth: 0
```

In GitLab CI set `GIT_DEPTH: 0`. Locally: `git fetch --unshallow`.

### "No commits found from … to …"
- Check the dates: `sprint.days` counts back from today, both days included.
- Merge commits are skipped. With squash or rebase merges that's fine. With merge commits, the work is in the merged branch's commits, which are included.
- Commits matching `ignore` are left out.
- In CI, make sure the branch you want is checked out, usually your main branch.

### "… of … commits not read" in checks.md
The sprint is longer than the model reads at once (`model.maxInputChars`). Every product commit still gets a line, so what's left out is usually docs and chores. If product commits are left out too, narrow `productPaths` or `ignore`, or raise `model.maxInputChars` when your model takes more.

### "Only the newest … commits were read"
The sprint has more commits than `limits.commits` (3,000), so its first days are missing. Raise the limit, or leave noise out with `ignore`.

### "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set"
Create a key at [console.anthropic.com](https://console.anthropic.com), then `export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...` in your shell or add it as a repository secret in CI.

### "Anthropic API 401"
The key is wrong or revoked. The tool doesn't try the fallback model for this.

### "Anthropic API 429" or "529"
Rate limited or overloaded. The tool retries three times with a pause, then tries the fallback model. Run it again a little later if it still fails.

### "The model returned nothing usable"
Every theme and the headline failed the checks, usually because the sprint has only tooling commits. Run with `--dry-run` to see which commits count as product work, and check `productPaths` and `nonProductTypes`.

### A theme I expected is missing
Look in `checks.md`. A point that named no real commit, or broke a rule, was dropped there. A theme that lost all its points was dropped too.

### Everything is under the hood
Your `productPaths` probably don't match. They're path prefixes from the repository root, such as `src/` or `apps/web/src/`. Run `--dry-run`: commits marked `[no product code]` didn't match.

### No before and after slides
- `screenshots.source` must be `git` or `folder`.
- With `git`, `dir` is a path from the repository root, and the PNGs must have changed during the sprint.
- A screen only gets a slide when the AI could say what changed. Tiny changes are skipped.
- Every screen looks changed because of the menu? Set `ignore.left` and `ignore.top`.

### The labels are in English but my content isn't
The fixed labels ship in English, Dutch, German, French and Spanish. For other languages, override them with `labels`. See [configuration](configuration.md#labels).

### The logo doesn't show
`brand.logo` must point to a PNG, JPG, SVG, WebP or GIF, relative to the config file. `doctor` checks that it exists.

### Still stuck?
[Open an issue](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/issues) with the output of `doctor` and `--dry-run`. Leave out anything private.

---

<!-- docs/faq.md -->

# FAQ

### Can I run it without sending anything outside our network?
Yes: use a local model with Ollama or LM Studio. The slides are plainer than with Claude, but nothing leaves your machine. See [models](models.md#ollama-local) and [security and privacy](security.md).

### Does it send my code to an AI?
No. It sends commit messages and file names of the sprint, pull request titles and descriptions when a GitHub token is set, plus your product description. Never source code, diffs, screenshots or usage numbers. See [what is sent](how-it-works.md#what-is-sent-to-the-ai).

### Which AI does it use?
Anthropic's Claude by default, through your own API key. Also Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini, Mistral, and local models with Ollama or LM Studio: see [models and providers](models.md). With the library you can plug in any model yourself ([custom model client](library.md#your-own-model-client)).

### What does it cost?
Two or three API calls per review (the third only when the second reader flagged lines to rewrite), on your own account. `--dry-run` shows the token estimate before you spend anything.

### Can it make things up?
It's built so it can't get away with it. Every point must name real commits from the sprint, or it's dropped. Numbers come from your files, never from the AI. Pictures can only be screenshots that exist. And a second AI reads the result like your audience would. A person still reads the draft before it's presented.

### My commit messages are bad. Will it still work?
Better messages give better slides, but it copes: it also reads the changed file names, and Conventional Commit prefixes help it sort tooling from product work. With a GitHub token it also reads the pull request descriptions, which usually say why.

### Do I need Conventional Commits?
No. They help (a `ci:` commit is never a theme), but anything works.

### Does it work with monorepos?
Yes. Set `productPaths` to the folders that hold product code, such as `apps/web/src/`.

### Can I use it for release notes instead of sprints?
Yes: `--from v1.4.0 --to v1.5.0`. `review.md` works well as release notes.

### Which languages?
The AI writes the content in any language. Slide labels ship in English, Dutch, German, French and Spanish; override them for others.

### Can I use my company's slide template?
Partly. Point `brand.from` at your PowerPoint and the deck takes its accent color, fonts and logo. The layout stays sprint-review's own; exporting into your own slide layouts is on the roadmap.

### Is there a hosted version?
No, on purpose. It runs where your code is, with your key, and produces a file. Nothing to sign up for, nothing to host.

### What does the deck need to open?
Any modern browser. No internet: everything is inside the one file.

### Can I edit the deck in PowerPoint or Keynote?
Yes: `--pptx` (or `output.pptx: true`) also writes `deck.pptx`, editable, with the speaker notes in the notes pane. Keynote opens it too.

### Is it free?
The tool is free and open source (MIT). You pay your model provider for the API calls.

### Why not just ask an AI to write the review?
You can, once. sprint-review does it every sprint with no one in the loop: it reads exactly the sprint's range, drops lines it can't trace to commits, diffs real screenshots, rewrites what a fresh reader didn't understand, and logs every correction. It also runs inside your AI assistant: see the [MCP server](integrations.md#claude-code-cursor-and-other-mcp-clients).

### Can I use it from Claude Code or Cursor?
Yes. `sprint-review mcp` is an MCP server, and there's a Claude Code skill. See [integrations](integrations.md).

---

<!-- docs/guides/how-to-run-a-sprint-review.md -->

# How to run a sprint review that people want to attend

A sprint review is where the team shows what it delivered and the people it delivers for react. In Scrum it's the second-to-last event of the sprint, before the retrospective. It's often the only moment the business, sales or management see the product move. Run well, it brings feedback that changes the next sprint. Run badly, it's a list of tickets nobody outside the team understands.

## Before: an hour of prep, not a day

1. **Collect what was done.** Merged pull requests and commits since the last review, not the sprint board's plan.
2. **Group it into a few themes.** Three to six themes the audience cares about ("customers can book repairs online"), not components ("refactor booking API").
3. **Say what each theme means for them.** One sentence of effect per theme: faster, fewer mistakes, less manual work, less risk, more insight.
4. **Show it.** A screenshot or a short live demo per theme. Before and after beats any description.
5. **Put plumbing in one place.** Dependency upgrades, CI and tests matter, but they belong on one *under the hood* slide.
6. **Add the bigger picture.** Where are you on the roadmap, and what moved in usage?

Steps 1 to 6 are what [sprint-review](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review) automates: it reads the git history, writes the themes in your audience's language, checks every line against the real commits, finds the screens that changed, and builds the deck.

## During: 30 to 60 minutes

- **Open with the sprint goal** and whether you reached it.
- **Demo, don't read.** The slide is the headline; the product is the story. Keep speaker notes for what to click.
- **Ask a question per theme.** "Would this change how you book a repair?" gets more useful feedback than "Any questions?"
- **Write down feedback as it comes.** It's input for the backlog.
- **End with what's next.** One slide: what the next sprint will likely pick up.

## After

- Share the deck and a short summary in the channel where the business lives.
- Turn feedback into backlog items before the next planning.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Instead |
|---|---|
| Showing ticket numbers and branch names | Plain-language themes and effects |
| Demoing everything | Three to six themes; the rest under the hood |
| A status meeting | Something to react to: working software |
| Slides prepared at the last minute | Generated from git before review day ([how](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review/blob/main/docs/github-action.md)) |

## Sprint review or retrospective?

The **sprint review** looks at the *product*: what was built, with the people it's for. The **retrospective** looks at the *way of working*, with the team only, right after. Different audiences, different questions; don't merge them.

---

<!-- docs/guides/sprint-review-template.md -->

# Sprint review template

A slide-by-slide structure for a sprint review that works for a non-technical audience. Use it by hand, or let [sprint-review](https://github.com/guuskeunen/sprint-review) fill it from your git history ([see a generated example](https://guuskeunen.github.io/sprint-review/demo/)).

| # | Slide | What goes on it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Cover** | Product, sprint dates, the sprint goal in one line |
| 2 | **What it brings** | The themes grouped by value: faster, better quality, less manual work, less risk, more insight |
| 3 | **In use** | Two to six numbers that moved, with last sprint for comparison |
| 4 | **This sprint in short** | Three to four one-line highlights |
| 5–10 | **One slide per theme** | A title of a few words, one sentence on the effect for the audience, two to four points, a screenshot; speaker notes on what to demo |
| 11–13 | **Before and after** | The screens that changed, side by side, with one line on what to look at |
| 14 | **Roadmap** | Milestones reached and open |
| 15 | **Under the hood** | Maintenance, upgrades, tests, CI: one slide |
| 16 | **Questions** | And what's next |

## Writing rules that make it land

- Write for the person in the room, not the person who wrote the code: "Front desk staff see a customer's whole history on one page", not "Added timeline endpoint".
- At most 16 words per point, 25 for the effect sentence.
- No ticket numbers, hashes or branch names on slides.
- Every claim must match something that was actually merged.

## Generate it instead

```bash
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review --dry-run   # see what it would read
npx @guuskeunen/sprint-review             # write the deck
```

The rules above are the checks sprint-review runs in code on every line.
